caption:
What happens if you stop getting treatments?
Less than the internet says, and more slowly.

Two different fears hide inside that question. One is that the effect fades and you drift back toward where you were heading anyway. The other is that you end up worse than if you had never started. People are usually afraid of the second while describing the first.

A case report followed identical twin sisters for 13 years, one treated regularly and one only twice. Lines visible at rest had not formed in the treated twin. Two people is not a trial and cannot give you a rate - but it carries its own control: the areas neither twin treated had aged the same amount in both faces.

Ask this before the first session rather than the last. What happens if I stop after a year? Does it fade, or does it need undoing? What am I left with if I never come back?

General education only.

#InformedConsent #AestheticConsultation #KoreanAesthetics #MedicalAesthetics #BetterDecisions
first_comment: Have you ever stopped something - and what actually happened? I ask because the answer people expect and the answer they report are usually not the same.

slides.alt_text: Slide 1 of 6: Two similar stones on wood, one polished, one weathered. If you stop, do you end up worse than before?
Slide 2 of 6: Three cards - going back, going below, the mix-up. Returning to baseline is not the same as damage.
Slide 3 of 6: Thirteen years, two identical twins, one treated regularly. A case report, not a trial, and its limits.
Slide 4 of 6: The stopping plan - name the exit, ask the shape, check the floor. Ask before the first session.
Slide 5 of 6: Four things that happen when people stop treatment, including that some of the change is simply age.
Slide 6 of 6: Fade, return, floor - three questions to answer before starting anything you may want to stop.
